account: The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) page “How we use data and analytics” states that the ATO uses machine learning, a common form of artificial intelligence. Nearest neighbor methods compare amounts being entered into myTax with those of other people in similar circumstances. If a claim is significantly different from what is expected, a message prompts the taxpayer to check the figures. The page reports that during tax time in 2020 nearly 340,000 taxpayers, around 7.5% of myTax users, received a pop-up message. The message suggested that they review a specific label. These prompts caused taxpayers to make adjustments estimated to have a revenue impact of around $37 million. The $37 million is the ATO's own estimate. The same page says that the ATO also uses machine-learning algorithms to forecast call-center volumes and speech recognition to transcribe inbound calls. Separately, in 2020 it automated 93,000 franking-credit refunds worth over $42 million for self-preparers over 60 (not described as machine learning). The page is undated, and the outcome concerns tax time 2020. An Internet Archive copy dated 14 July 2021 contains the 340,000 and $37 million figures. The Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) audit of 24 February 2025 found that the real-time analytics component uses nearest neighbor analysis at lodgment. It found that the ATO did not document the weights behind that component. The Mandarin reported on 25 February 2025 that the ANAO found that the ATO's governance arrangements for artificial intelligence were only partly effective. The report gives no outcome figures. No source independent of the ATO gives a recovered figure attributable to machine learning. In its State of the Service Report 2024-25, the Australian Public Service Commission (APSC) reported ATO figures of over 712,000 prompts and an estimated $92.6 million of revenue protected for the 2023-24 income year. It also reported that an ATO randomized trial found that nudged taxpayers were 3 times more likely to adjust their data than taxpayers without a message.

ai_role.statement: The models compare each claim with the claims of similar taxpayers and decide which claims trigger a message. The taxpayer then decides whether to change the figure. The ATO's randomized trial compares taxpayers who received a message with taxpayers who did not, so it measures the effect of the message. It does not compare model-selected prompts with prompts chosen by simple rules. The ANAO found that the ATO did not document the weights behind the real-time analytics model, and its audit does not test the revenue estimates.

fields.account: The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) page “How we use data and analytics” states that the ATO uses machine learning, a common form of artificial intelligence. Nearest neighbor methods compare amounts being entered into myTax with those of other people in similar circumstances. If a claim is significantly different from what is expected, a message prompts the taxpayer to check the figures. The page reports that during tax time in 2020 nearly 340,000 taxpayers, around 7.5% of myTax users, received a pop-up message. The message suggested that they review a specific label. These prompts caused taxpayers to make adjustments estimated to have a revenue impact of around $37 million. The $37 million is the ATO's own estimate. The same page says that the ATO also uses machine-learning algorithms to forecast call-center volumes and speech recognition to transcribe inbound calls. Separately, in 2020 it automated 93,000 franking-credit refunds worth over $42 million for self-preparers over 60 (not described as machine learning). The page is undated, and the outcome concerns tax time 2020. An Internet Archive copy dated 14 July 2021 contains the 340,000 and $37 million figures. The Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) audit of 24 February 2025 found that the real-time analytics component uses nearest neighbor analysis at lodgment. It found that the ATO did not document the weights behind that component. The Mandarin reported on 25 February 2025 that the ANAO found that the ATO's governance arrangements for artificial intelligence were only partly effective. The report gives no outcome figures. No source independent of the ATO gives a recovered figure attributable to machine learning. In its State of the Service Report 2024-25, the Australian Public Service Commission (APSC) reported ATO figures of over 712,000 prompts and an estimated $92.6 million of revenue protected for the 2023-24 income year. It also reported that an ATO randomized trial found that nudged taxpayers were 3 times more likely to adjust their data than taxpayers without a message.
fields.summary: At tax time 2020, nearest-neighbor checks in the Australian Taxation Office's myTax prompted nearly 340,000 users to review a claim; the office puts the revenue impact at about $37 million.
